body: We try not to use the C++ standard library much in Godot. Use `HashMap` or `AHashMap` instead of `std::map`, `HashSet` instead of `std::set`, and `LocalVector` instead of `std::vector` (unless you're passing it around, in which case use the refcounted `Vector` instead).
This calculation of stiffness has changed since you copied it over.

I'm not sure if this is necessarily a good lead to follow, but note that scene nodes don't currently reference `PhysicsServer3D` enums like this. If you look at the code for the `Area3D` node you'll see that it declares its own `SpaceOverride` enum, while the physics server has its own `AreaSpaceOverrideMode`.

Yes, this means they can technically go out of sync, and we should probably address that in some way, but for the sake of consistency you'll probably want to do the same, otherwise people need to prefix the enum entries with `PhysicsServer3D` in a `SoftBody3D` script.

Calling this `soft_body_form` when it's in the `SoftBody3D` node seems a bit verbose/redundant. Maybe just `form` is fine instead? Same goes for the getter/setter, as well as the stuff in `JoltSoftBody3D`.

body:
I wanted to use an enum since there could potentially be other ways to analyze the mesh in the future.  For example, I was thinking of maybe adding a convex hull variation in addition to the current one that conforms to the input mesh.  In any case, using a bool locks you into only ever having two states.
---
Edit:
Also, lexically, this isn't really a boolean choice like turning a light on or off or making a mesh visible or invisible.  This is setting how the mesh is meant to be interpreted, which to me sounds more like an enum, even if there are only two choices at the moment.

I was copying the neighbouring methods which have the same form.  `ERR_FAIL_NULL_V` also seems to require the `soft_body` pointer.  I'm returning the cloth value since "cloth" is the same as how Godot behaved before I made this PR.

I could add an extra enum, but there are other methods that use `PhysicsServer3D` enums directly like `PhysicsBody3D::set_axis_lock(PhysicsServer3D::BodyAxis p_axis, bool p_lock)`. 

The value is being stored on the physics object itself, so creating a separate enum that only exists on `SoftBody3D` would just be adding an extra layer of indirection.  Also, if you follow the logic of how `Area3D` handles `SpaceOverride`, I think it's just depending on the enum values being identical to `AreaSpaceOverrideMode`.  The code is also bit convoluted.

All comments in godot seem to be of the form:

```
// Comment
```

and not

```
//Comment
```
Add some tolerance to prevent tiny slivers? (tiny slivers will be very destructive to the sim)
These two lines seem redundant
Instead of doing a ray cast (very expensive), could you use your connectivity information and create triangles for tetrahedrons without neighbors?
This function will not set the compliance on your `Volume` constraints. This means it will be 0 and incredibly stiff. This is probably why you have stability issues.
This is a lot of comment/code to copy paste. Split off to a helper function?
You will need to update the `Volume::mSixRestVolume` values too in this case. A simple fix is to move the call to `CalculateVolumeConstraintVolumes` below this loop.

The issue with that is requires meshes to be manifold.  Real would user data may not be, such as the default monkey model in Blender.  Using ray casting still gives you reasonable results in a non manifold model while an adjacency-filled algorithm will return an empty space.

I was also looking at the code for another tetrahedraizer and it used this method.  And `TriangleMesh` uses a BVH tree, so it does have some optimization.

I could snap together points that are within an epsilon of each other, but I think I'd need to add a specialized BVH tree into the code to handle that efficiently.  Or we could argue it's the responsibility of the user to provide a valid mesh.  Maybe SoftBody3D should be changed so that the visual mesh is separate from the collision mesh?

Also, Delaunay tetrahedralizations will naturally produce a lot of slivers.  I might need to write my own Delaunay algorithm after all to handle this, but I think the one Godot has is good enough for now.
Does `settings->CalculateEdgeLengths();` need to be above or below this loop?

How would I set compliance for volumes?  `SoftBodySharedSettings::CreateConstraints` only accepts the `VertexAttributes`.  I don't see anything similar I could use to set volume constrains.

Also, should this require adding an extra parameter to SoftBody3D so the user can adjust the volume stiffness?  Or does it follow from the stiffness for the edges?
`auto` is [not allowed](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/cpp_usage_guidelines.html#auto-keyword)
Same here

Separating the visual mesh from the collision mesh is a good idea and probably required if we want to make this feature useful for anything but toy projects. Usually, you have to use a simulation mesh that is of much lower quality than the render mesh, so I don't think it's just about snapping vertices that are close. Eventually we want the user to be able to specify 2 completely different meshes. Each render vertex can then be attached to the closest tetrahedron (and deform with it) to go from sim to render mesh. Alternatively, we automatically create a low res sim mesh from a high res render mesh (there are various papers on this subject).

> Also, should this require adding an extra parameter to SoftBody3D so the user can adjust the volume stiffness? Or does it follow from the stiffness for the edges?

You can use the same value, but having 2 values allows you to specify volume preservation and edge length preservation seperately.

Would you want to have some sort of skinning from the deformation mesh to the visual mesh?  I think most skeletal systems use a weighted sum of the 4 most influential bones for each point.  You could automatically set this up so each vertex in the low res mesh counts as a bone and build a mapping to the visual mesh vertices based on proximity.  Maybe even find a way to work this into the existing skeleton system?  But that is going beyond what this PR is about.
In any case, I think the best way to deal with slivers is adding Steiner points to the delaunay tetrahedralization (which I'm still reading up on) rather than snapping together close verts.

Okay, that's a lot more stable now.  Would you know how I could change how soft it is - ie, make it act something like a pillow?  Right now it bounces like a rubber ball.  If I turn the Linear Stiffness down, it looks like some of the volume is turning inside out.  If I turn it way down, the simulation blows up.

I don't really know how you can achieve this effect. 

* Having different compliance value for the volumes and edges probably helps.
* I haven't looked at what your tetrahedrons look like, but I think they only use the original triangles of the model, which probably means that they're not really uniform in size. You probably need a grid like arrangement of the tetrahedrons (which also means generating vertices and edges in the interior) to get better simulation quality.
